title: Outward occasions counted as rousing grace (Valencia, Alvarez)
source_text: XXXVIII. Imo quanquam auxilium illud speciale, quod in excitans & adjuvans dividunt, in internis animi motibus, ut dictum est, proprie consistat; multi tamen ad gratiam excitantem revocant etiam externa quaedam: ut sunt occasiones & opportunitates, quas divina providentia suppeditat homini, ut in eo excitentur hujusmodi motus, tam in intellectu, quam in appetitu. Cujusmodi sunt infirmitas, pericula, boni socii, adversitates, & alii varii eventus: sicut videre est apud Gregorium de Valentia loco modo citato. Et similiter Alvares notat gratiam excitantem comprehendere excitationem, tum externam, quae fit per creaturas & signa sensibilia; tum etiam internam, quae fit a Deo immediate, quum immittit pias cogitationes, & proponit ea quae inducere possunt liberum arbitrium ad actum fidei & charitatis, & alias supernaturales operationes. De auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 8. disp. 75.
pass_a_gloss: XXXVIII. Indeed although that special help, which they divide into rousing and helping, consists properly in internal motions of the soul, as has been said; many however refer to rousing grace also certain external things: as are occasions and opportunities, which divine providence supplies to man, that in him motions of this kind may be excited, as well in the intellect, as in the appetite. Of which kind are sickness, dangers, good companions, adversities, and other various events: as is to be seen in Gregory of Valencia in the place just cited. And similarly Alvarez notes that rousing grace comprehends excitation, both external, which happens through creatures and sensible signs; and also internal, which happens from God immediately, when he sends in pious thoughts, and proposes those things which can induce free choice to the act of faith and charity, and other supernatural operations. De auxiliis divinae gratiae book 8 disp. 75.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXVIII. Indeed, although that special help, which they divide into rousing and assisting, strictly consists in inward movements of the soul, as has been said, many also count certain outward things as rousing grace. These are the occasions and opportunities that God's providence supplies to a person so that such movements may be stirred in him, in both the intellect and the appetite.
Examples are sickness, dangers, good companions, misfortunes and various other events, as may be seen in Gregory of Valencia at the place just cited.

Alvarez likewise notes that rousing grace includes both an outward rousing, which comes through creatures and signs perceived by the senses, and an inward one, which comes directly from God when he puts devout thoughts into the mind and sets before it what can lead free choice to the act of faith and charity and to other supernatural works (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 8, disputation 75).
